22.title: The white elephant dream
22.hook: Queen Maya dreams a white elephant enters her side; the wise men say a great son is coming
22.howItsDone: Buddhists remember Maya's dream in temple murals, carvings and festival plays; in many countries the story is told to children as the first chapter of the Buddha's life, and the white elephant remains a symbol of blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Dhammapada, and camp one closed with twenty-one words. Your line: what you think, you become.
screen: `THE DHAMMAPADA — WHAT YOU THINK, YOU BECOME.`

segments.voice: Night, in Kapilavatthu, a city at the foot of the Himalayas. It's the time of a summer festival. Queen Maya, wife of King Suddhodana, has kept the festival well, given gifts, and gone to sleep. She dreams that a white elephant, shining like silver, walks toward her, circles her bed, and enters her side. The Buddha's life story begins here, one scene at a time.
screen: `A CITY BELOW THE MOUNTAINS.` → `A QUEEN DREAMS OF AN ELEPHANT.` → `THE STORY BEGINS.`

segments.voice: In the later tellings, guardian spirits carry Maya up to a high place in the mountains, bathe her in a lake, and lay her on a heavenly couch. A white elephant with six tusks, a white lotus in its trunk, comes down from a golden mountain, trumpets, walks around her three times, and seems to enter her right side. In the morning she tells the king. He calls in the brahmins, the wise men who read signs. Be glad, they say. The queen has conceived, and it's a son. If he stays in the household, he'll be a great king who rules the world. If he leaves it, he'll be a buddha: one who wakes up and removes the veil from the world. Where does this come from? The early discourses describe his conception with wonders, a great light, the earth trembling, but no elephant. The dream comes from later biographies and commentaries, and it's old in its own right: the scene is carved in stone at early Buddhist sites in India, such as Bharhut. Why an elephant? In ancient India a white elephant was a royal treasure, rare and auspicious: strength, gentleness and greatness at once. Across Buddhist Asia the dream is painted on temple walls, and in Thailand and Myanmar the white elephant is still a sign of blessing. Before anyone knows who this child will be, something announces him.

23.title: Born in a grove
23.hook: on the road to her parents' home, Maya gives birth holding a branch in the Lumbini garden
23.howItsDone: Buddhists celebrate the Buddha's birth at Vesak, or in East Asia on a birthday festival in spring, often by pouring sweet water or tea over a small statue of the newborn Buddha; Lumbini, in Nepal, is one of the four great pilgrimage places.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the white elephant, a queen's dream, and a son foretold. Some things announce themselves.

Queen Maya is heavily pregnant, and she wants to go home. Not to the palace: to her parents' home in a town called Devadaha, the way many women of her time went back to their mothers to give birth. The king has the road smoothed and decorated, and she sets out in a golden palanquin with a crowd of attendants. Halfway there, the road passes a grove of sal trees in full bloom: flowers everywhere, bees humming, birds singing. She asks to stop and walk in the garden a while. She never makes it to her mother's house.
screen: `MAYA WANTS TO GO HOME.` → `A GROVE IN FULL BLOOM.` → `SHE NEVER ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: The grove is called Lumbini. As the story is told, the queen walks to a great sal tree and reaches up, and the branch bends down to her hand. Standing there, holding it, she gives birth. No palace, no bed, no midwives from court. The wonders are older still, from the early discourses: the child is received first by gods, two streams of water fall from the sky to wash mother and son, and the baby stands, takes seven steps, looks in every direction, and says this is his last birth. Every Buddhist tradition tells some form of this scene, and in many temples an image of the newborn, one hand pointing up and one down, is bathed with sweet water on his birthday. Now the part that isn't legend. A century or two after the Buddha's death, depending on whose dating you follow, the emperor Ashoka, who had become a Buddhist, came to Lumbini on pilgrimage and set up a stone pillar. Its inscription says, in effect, that here the Buddha, the sage of the Sakyas, was born, and that because of this the village's taxes were lowered. Lost for centuries, the pillar was found again in eighteen ninety-six. It still stands in southern Nepal, and pilgrims from all over the world walk there. A real place, a real stone, and a story about arriving before you arrive: the most important birth in the tradition happened on the road, under a tree, on the way somewhere else.

Then close your eyes and let the breath be your garden.

24.title: The old sage weeps
24.hook: the sage Asita holds the baby, smiles, then weeps: he will not live to hear this child teach
24.howItsDone: Buddhists tell the story of Asita as part of the Buddha's birth, and in Theravada communities the Nalaka Sutta is recited and studied; the scene of Asita holding the infant appears in temple art across Asia.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lumbini, a birth in a garden on the road between two homes. Born on the way somewhere.

Gods in the sky, the story says, celebrating: waving their cloaks, shouting for joy. An old seer named Asita, resting in his daytime retreat, sees them and asks why. They tell him: in the land of the Sakyas, a child has been born who will one day turn the wheel of the teaching. So the old man hurries to King Suddhodana's palace and asks to see the baby. The king brings the child out, and Asita takes him in his arms.
screen: `THE GODS ARE CELEBRATING.` → `AN OLD SEER HURRIES TO THE PALACE.` → `HE HOLDS THE BABY.`

segments.voice: This story is told in verse, in a collection called the Sutta Nipata. Asita holds the baby and looks at him closely, the way an expert looks at something rare. He reads the marks on the child's body, and he's sure. Joyful, he lifts his voice: this one is supreme, the highest among people. Then, holding the child, the old man starts to cry. The Sakyans are frightened. Is something wrong with the baby? Is danger coming? No, Asita tells them. Nothing bad will happen to this child. He'll reach the highest awakening, teach out of compassion for many, and his way of life will spread far. I'm weeping for myself. My life is nearly over. I'll be gone before he teaches, and I won't be there to hear it. It's a strange, tender moment this early in the story: the one who sees clearly who this child is knows he'll never see it come true. But Asita doesn't only grieve. He goes to his nephew, a young man named Nalaka, and tells him: when you hear that someone has awakened and is teaching, go to him. Follow him. Years later, the story says, Nalaka does. The old man couldn't reach the future himself, so he sent someone into it: a seed planted in a garden he knew he'd never walk in.

25.title: Seven days
25.hook: Maya dies a week after the birth; her sister Mahapajapati raises him as her own
25.howItsDone: Buddhists honor both Maya, the Buddha's mother, and Mahapajapati Gotami, who raised him; Mahapajapati is remembered as the first Buddhist nun, and Buddhist teaching stresses gratitude to parents and those who raise us.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Asita, the old seer who wept because he'd never hear the child teach, and sent his nephew instead. Plant it anyway.

Queen Maya dies. Until now the story has been all wonders: a shining elephant in a dream, a branch bending to a queen's hand, gods cheering in the sky, a sage weeping over a cradle. It read like a fairy tale, and fairy tales don't usually turn this hard. The baby everyone says will change the world is one week old, and he has no mother.
screen: `QUEEN MAYA DIES.` → `UNTIL NOW, ALL WONDERS.` → `THE BABY HAS NO MOTHER.`

segments.voice: A discourse says it plainly, as if it were simply part of the pattern: seven days after a future buddha is born, his mother dies. No long scene. It adds one line: she reappears in a heaven, the Tusita heaven. A later story tells of the Buddha, years afterward, going to teach her among the gods. But on earth a newborn has lost his mother, and here's who steps in: Maya's younger sister, Mahapajapati Gotami. She's also married to King Suddhodana, and she has a baby son of her own, Nanda. The commentaries say she gives her own son to nurses and nurses Siddhattha herself, raising him as her own. Years later it's remembered out loud. In one discourse, Mahapajapati brings the Buddha a gift of new cloth, and his attendant Ananda speaks up for her. She was his mother's sister, Ananda says, his nurse, his foster mother; she nursed him when his own mother died. A debt of care, said in front of everyone. Her own story doesn't end there; she'll come back later on this path, with a story of her own. Today is about a child whose first great loss came before he could remember it, and a woman who chose to love him as if he were hers. The tradition keeps them both: the mother who carried him, and the mother who raised him.

26.title: The one whose aim succeeds
26.hook: the naming; the brahmins read the marks: a great king or a great teacher
26.howItsDone: Buddhists know the Buddha as Siddhattha Gotama, or Siddhartha Gautama, and as Sakyamuni, the sage of the Sakyas; the naming and the reading of the marks are told in temple art and in stories for children.

segments.voice: Yesterday: seven days. Maya died a week after the birth, and her sister raised him. Love can be adopted.

Somebody chose your name. Maybe after a grandparent, maybe from a book, maybe because it sounded good with your last name. Every name carries a little wish. Today the baby in the palace gets his. The king invites a hundred and eight brahmins to a feast, the story says, to name the child and to tell his future. Eight of them are the wisest. And they don't all agree.
screen: `SOMEONE CHOSE YOUR NAME.` → `A FEAST FOR THE NAMING.` → `EIGHT WISE MEN DISAGREE.`

segments.voice: They name him Siddhattha, in Pali, or Siddhartha, the Sanskrit form more familiar in English. Siddha means accomplished, succeeded. Attha means aim, goal, purpose. So: the one whose aim succeeds. Gotama is the family name, and the Sakyas are his people, which is why he's later called Sakyamuni, the sage of the Sakyas. Then the eight brahmins read his body. Buddhist texts describe thirty-two marks of a great man, signs a trained eye was said to recognize. In the later tellings, seven of them raise two fingers: two possibilities. If he stays home, he'll be a king who rules the whole world. If he leaves home, he'll be a buddha. The same prophecy his parents heard after the dream. But the youngest of the eight, Kondañña, raises one finger. He says there's only one road for this child: he will leave, and become a buddha. Hold on to that name; Kondañña comes back much later, at a very important moment. Now stand where the king stands. One road leads to an empire, his son on the throne, the family's future secure. The other leads out the palace gate, and away. You can guess which a father would hope for, and that hope will shape everything the king does for years. For now, the baby just has a name: a wish, and, the story says, a promise.

27.title: The rose-apple tree
27.hook: at the plowing festival the boy sits in the shade and falls into a quiet joy (MN 36)
27.howItsDone: Buddhists develop jhana through concentration meditation, often on the breath; it is taught in Theravada meditation traditions as the four absorptions, and the word itself, through Sanskrit dhyana and Chinese chan, gave Zen its name.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Siddhattha, the one whose aim succeeds, and Kondañña's single raised finger. A name is a wish.

The plowing festival. The whole town is out in the fields: music, food, bright clothes, oxen with decorated horns, and the king himself takes hold of a golden plow to open the season. Everyone watches the king. Nobody watches the boy. His nurses have set him down in the shade of a rose-apple tree at the edge of the field and wandered off to see the show. Alone, the boy sits cross-legged, quiet. And something happens that he'll remember for the rest of his life.
screen: `THE PLOWING FESTIVAL.` → `EVERYONE WATCHES THE KING.` → `A BOY UNDER A TREE.`

segments.voice: The festival details come from later tellings, but the heart of this story is the Buddha's own, from a discourse where he looks back on his search. He's describing the punishing practices of those years, the fasting and the strain, and how they got him nowhere. At his lowest point, he remembers: when his father was working in the fields, he sat in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree and entered a quiet joy, secluded from wanting, secluded from anything unwholesome, with a happiness born of that seclusion. He calls it the first jhana. Could that be the way to awakening? he wonders, and realizes it is. Then comes the question that turns his whole search around: why am I afraid of that kind of happiness, one that has nothing to do with the pleasures of the senses? Jhana means deep meditative absorption: the mind settling, gathering, becoming still and bright. The texts describe four levels, each quieter than the last. And a surprise: the Pali jhana is dhyana in Sanskrit. When Buddhism reached China, dhyana became chan. In Japan, chan became zen. The name Zen comes from this word. For the Buddha, the point wasn't the joy itself. It was the memory. Peace wasn't something he had to force, starve for or conquer. He'd found it by himself, as a child, doing nothing, in the shade.
screen: `THE BUDDHA REMEMBERS THE TREE.` · `THE FIRST JHANA: A QUIET JOY.` · `WHY AM I AFRAID OF THAT HAPPINESS?` · `JHANA, DHYANA, CHAN, ZEN.` · then, large: `YOU'VE BEEN HERE BEFORE.`

segments.voice: If you can, sit somewhere shady: under a tree, by a window, in a quiet corner. Do nothing, not even meditating, exactly; be still the way a child is when nobody's watching, and let the breath do what it does. If a little ease shows up, a small quiet pleasure in simply being here, don't be afraid of it: let it stay.
Jhana. Meditative absorption: the mind gathered, still and bright. Dhyana in Sanskrit, the root of chan and zen.

28.title: The swan
28.hook: a later telling: cousin Devadatta shoots a swan, Siddhattha tends it, and the court says it belongs to the one who saved it
28.carry: life belongs to who protects it
28.howItsDone: Buddhists tell the swan story to children as an example of compassion toward animals; many Buddhists practice releasing or protecting animals, and some keep a vegetarian diet out of the same concern for living beings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: jhana, the quiet joy under the rose-apple tree, and the word behind Zen. You've been here before.

Two boys, cousins, in the palace gardens. A flock of swans flies overhead, white against the sky. One of the cousins has a bow. He draws it and shoots, and a swan falls out of the sky, an arrow through its wing. It's the last childhood story after a week of them: a queen's dream of a white elephant, a birth in a garden on the road, an old sage in tears, a mother lost at seven days and a mother who stayed, a name that's a wish, a boy at peace under a tree. Millions of children have heard this one.
screen: `SWANS OVERHEAD.` → `AN ARROW, AND ONE FALLS.` → `A WEEK OF STORIES ENDS.`

segments.voice: The cousin with the bow is Devadatta. Remember that name; he'll be back, and not kindly. The swan lands near Siddhattha, who gets there first. He kneels, gently pulls out the arrow, and holds the bird against himself to calm it, tending the wound. Devadatta runs up. That's my swan. I shot it. Give it to me. No, says Siddhattha. It isn't yours. You tried to kill it. I saved it. The boys can't settle it, so, the story goes, they take it to the court, to the wise men. Both sides are heard. The hunter says: I brought it down, so it's mine. The healer says: I kept it alive, so it's in my care. The court decides: a life belongs to the one who saves it, not the one who tries to take it. The swan goes with Siddhattha, who looks after it until it can fly, and then lets it go. To be honest about this one: it isn't in the oldest Buddhist texts. It's a later telling, made famous in the West by a long English poem, The Light of Asia, published by Edwin Arnold in eighteen seventy-nine. But it's loved across the Buddhist world, in picture books, school plays and temple paintings, because it says something the whole tradition believes. The first precept is not to harm living beings, and here it is in a child, before anyone taught him. And look at the judgment. Not might makes right. Care makes right.
screen: `DEVADATTA SHOOTS. SIDDHATTHA KNEELS.` · `THAT'S MY SWAN.` · `THE COURT: IT'S THE SAVER'S.` · `A LATER TELLING, WIDELY LOVED.` · then, large: `LIFE BELONGS TO WHO PROTECTS IT.`

segments.voice: Picture one small living thing near you: a plant, a pet, a bird at the feeder, an insect you might carry outside. See yourself tending it slowly, with the same gentle hands the boy used with the swan. Then rest in the breath and let a little metta go to that small life.
The swan. Devadatta shot it, Siddhattha saved it, and the court said a life belongs to the one who protects it.
Your line: life belongs to who protects it. Not the hunter's: the healer's. That's week four.
